title: Book VI: The Widow And The Wife — Chapter LIX
paragraphs:
“They said of old the Soul had human shape,
But smaller, subtler than the fleshly self,
So wandered forth for airing when it pleased.
And see! beside her cherub-face there floats
A pale-lipped form aerial whispering
Its promptings in that little shell her ear.”

News often spreads as carelessly and effectively as the pollen bees carry away, unaware of how dusty they are, while buzzing after their own particular nectar. This elegant comparison concerns Fred Vincy. That evening at Lowick Parsonage, he heard the ladies eagerly discussing news their old servant had obtained from Tantripp: Mr. Casaubon’s strange reference to Mr. Ladislaw in a codicil added to his will shortly before his death. Miss Winifred was astonished that her brother already knew. She declared Camden extraordinary at knowing things and never telling them. Mary Garth suggested the codicil had perhaps become mixed up with spiders’ habits, which Miss Winifred refused to hear about. Mrs. Farebrother thought the news explained why they had seen Mr. Ladislaw at Lowick only once. Miss Noble made a series of small, compassionate mewing sounds.

Fred knew little about Ladislaw and the Casaubons and cared less. He never thought of the conversation again until, stopping at Rosamond’s one day to deliver a message for his mother, he happened to see Ladislaw leaving. Since marriage had freed Rosamond from the unpleasantness of living with brothers, she and Fred had little to say to one another. They had still less now that he had taken what she considered the foolish, even blameworthy step of abandoning the Church for work such as Mr. Garth’s. Fred therefore preferred to discuss news he thought neutral. “Speaking of that young Ladislaw,” he repeated what he had heard at Lowick Parsonage.

Like Mr. Farebrother, Lydgate knew far more than he told. Once he began considering the relationship between Will and Dorothea, his guesses went beyond the facts. He imagined a passionate attachment on both sides, which seemed far too serious for gossip. Remembering Will’s irritability when Mrs. Casaubon had been mentioned made him still more cautious. Taken together, what he knew and what he guessed increased his friendliness and patience toward Ladislaw. They helped him understand the indecision that kept Will in Middlemarch after announcing he would leave. It showed how separate Lydgate’s mind was from Rosamond’s that he felt no impulse to discuss it with her. Indeed, he did not entirely trust her to remain discreet with Will. On that point he was right, though he could not have imagined how her thoughts would push her to speak.
When she repeated Fred’s news, Lydgate said, “Rosy, don’t let even the slightest hint of this slip to Ladislaw. He’s likely to flare up as though you’d insulted him. Naturally, it’s painful.”

Rosamond turned her head and patted her hair, looking perfectly calm and indifferent. But the next time Will visited while Lydgate was away, she teased him about not having gone to London as he had threatened.
“I know everything. A confidential little bird told me,” she said, tilting her head prettily over the work she held up between her busy fingers. “There’s a powerful magnet nearby.”
“There certainly is. Nobody knows that better than you,” Will answered with light gallantry, though inwardly ready to be angry.

“It’s the most delightful romance. Mr. Casaubon jealous, realizing there was no one Mrs. Casaubon would rather marry, and no one more eager to marry her than a certain gentleman. Then he makes a plan to ruin everything by taking away her property if she marries that gentleman. And then—and then—and then—oh, I’m sure the ending will be wonderfully romantic.”
“Good God! What are you talking about?” Will said. His face and ears flushed, and his features seemed altered, as if he had been violently shaken. “Stop joking. Tell me what you mean.”
“You really don’t know?” Rosamond asked. Her playfulness vanished. She wanted nothing more than to tell him and see the effects.
“I don’t!” he replied impatiently.
“You don’t know Mr. Casaubon’s will says Mrs. Casaubon loses all her property if she marries you?”
“How do you know it’s true?” Will demanded eagerly.
“My brother Fred heard it from the Farebrothers.” Will sprang from his chair and reached for his hat.
“I expect she prefers you to the property,” Rosamond said, watching him from a distance.
“Please say no more,” Will answered in a low, hoarse voice unlike his usual light one. “It’s a vile insult to her and to me.” Absently he sat down again, staring ahead without seeing anything.
“Now you’re angry with _me_,” Rosamond said. “It’s very unfair to blame _me_. You ought to thank me for telling you.”
“I do,” Will answered abruptly, with the divided awareness of someone replying to questions while dreaming.
“I shall expect news of the wedding,” Rosamond said playfully.
“Never! You’ll never hear of that wedding!”
After blurting out those words, Will stood, offered Rosamond his hand with the same sleepwalking air, and left.

Once he was gone, Rosamond rose and crossed the room. She leaned against a small cabinet and looked wearily out of the window. Boredom oppressed her, along with that dissatisfaction which in women’s minds so often turns into petty jealousy. It rests on no actual claim and grows from no deeper passion than the vague demands of self-interest, yet it can drive actions as well as words. “There really isn’t anything worth caring much about,” poor Rosamond thought. She remembered the family at Quallingham, who did not write, and considered that Tertius might come home and bother her about expenses. She had already secretly disobeyed him by asking her father for assistance. His final, decisive answer had been, “I’m more likely to need help myself.”
